questions.text: What term describes the basic economic problem that resources are limited but people's wants are unlimited? Give the term.
questions.solution: Scarcity means there are not enough resources to satisfy all wants, so choices must be made
questions.hint: There is not enough of everything to go round

questions.text: What term describes the next best alternative given up when a choice is made? Give the term.
questions.solution: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone
questions.hint: It is the 'cost' of the chance you missed

questions.text: Which of these is a factor of production?

options: Labour
Profit
Demand
Inflation
feedback: Profit is the reward for enterprise, not a factor itself

questions.solution: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and enterprise
questions.hint: Factors of production are the resources used to make goods and services

questions.text: What does the law of demand state?

options: As price rises, quantity demanded rises
As price rises, quantity demanded falls (other things being equal)
As price falls, quantity supplied rises
Price has no effect on quantity demanded

questions.solution: The demand curve slopes downwards: a higher price means a lower quantity demanded, other things being equal
questions.hint: Think about the shape of a demand curve

questions.text: What is the name for the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied? Give the term.
questions.solution: At the equilibrium (market-clearing) price there is no excess demand or excess supply
questions.hint: The market is 'balanced' at this price

questions.text: Which factor of production is rewarded with profit?

options: Land
Labour
Enterprise
Capital
feedback: Land earns rent
Labour earns wages
Capital earns interest

questions.solution: Land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest and enterprise earns profit
questions.hint: Which factor takes the risk of starting a business?

questions.text: What causes a movement along a demand curve, rather than a shift of the curve?

options: A change in consumers' incomes
A change in tastes and fashions
A change in the price of a substitute
A change in the good's own price
feedback: A change in income shifts the demand curve
A change in tastes shifts the demand curve
A change in a substitute's price shifts the demand curve

questions.solution: A change in the good's own price moves along the curve; changes in other factors (income, tastes, related goods) shift it
questions.hint: Which variable is on the axis of the demand diagram?

questions.text: Which pair of goods are complements?

options: Printers and ink cartridges
Tea and coffee
Butter and margarine
Buses and trains
feedback: Tea and coffee are substitutes
Butter and margarine are substitutes
Buses and trains are substitutes

questions.solution: Complements are used together, so demand for one rises when the other gets cheaper; the others are substitutes
questions.hint: Complements are bought and used together

questions.text: Which is a feature of a public good?

options: It is always sold at a high price
It is non-excludable: people cannot easily be stopped from using it
It is only provided by private firms
One person using it stops others from using it
feedback: Public goods are non-rival: one person's use does not reduce what is left for others

questions.solution: Public goods are non-excludable and non-rival (e.g. street lighting), which leads to the free-rider problem
questions.hint: Think about street lighting: can anyone be stopped from using it?

questions.text: Which is an example of a negative externality?

options: A firm earning a high profit
A consumer paying a high price for a good
Noise from a factory that disturbs nearby residents
A worker being paid a wage

questions.solution: A negative externality is a cost to a third party, such as noise or pollution affecting people not involved in the trade
questions.hint: Look for a cost that falls on people outside the transaction

questions.text: What term describes a good whose demand rises when consumers' incomes rise? Give the term.

feedback.inferior good: Demand for an inferior good FALLS when incomes rise
feedback.inferior goods: Demand for an inferior good FALLS when incomes rise
feedback.inferior: Demand for an inferior good FALLS when incomes rise

questions.solution: For a normal good, demand rises as income rises; for an inferior good, demand falls as income rises
questions.hint: This is the usual reaction: more income, more demand

questions.text: What term describes the situation when quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied at the current price? Give the term.

feedback.excess supply: Excess supply is when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded
feedback.surplus: A surplus is when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded

questions.solution: Excess demand (a shortage) puts upward pressure on the price until the market clears
questions.hint: There is not enough supply for everyone who wants to buy

questions.text: Petrol prices rise sharply. What is likely to happen to the demand for large cars that use a lot of petrol?

options: Demand rises (the demand curve shifts right)
Supply of large cars falls to zero
Nothing, because the goods are unrelated
Demand falls (the demand curve shifts left)

questions.solution: Petrol and cars are complements, so dearer petrol reduces demand for petrol-hungry cars
questions.hint: Are petrol and cars used together?

questions.text: A frost destroys much of the orange harvest. What happens in the market for oranges?

options: Supply falls, so the price rises
Supply rises, so the price falls
Demand rises, so supply falls
Demand falls, so the price rises

questions.solution: Supply shifts left; at the old price there is excess demand, so the price rises
questions.hint: Is this a change in supply or in demand?

questions.text: A government places a tax on cigarettes. What is the main aim?

options: To increase consumption of a merit good
To reduce consumption of a demerit good
To lower the price of cigarettes
To turn cigarettes into a public good
feedback: Merit goods (such as education) are under-consumed — cigarettes are the opposite

questions.solution: Cigarettes are a demerit good that is over-consumed; a tax raises the price and reduces consumption
questions.hint: Do governments want people to consume more or fewer cigarettes?

questions.text: A student chooses to work a Saturday shift instead of going to a football match with friends. What is the opportunity cost of working?

options: The wages earned from the shift
The cost of travel to work
Going to the football match
The tax paid on the wages
feedback: The wages are the benefit of working, not the cost

questions.solution: The opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up: the football match
questions.hint: What did the student give up?

questions.text: As people's incomes rise, demand for a supermarket's cheapest own-brand bread falls. What type of good is this bread? Give the term.

feedback.normal good: Demand for a normal good RISES when incomes rise
feedback.normal: Demand for a normal good RISES when incomes rise

questions.solution: When demand falls as income rises, the good is an inferior good: people switch to better-quality alternatives
questions.hint: Demand moves in the opposite direction to income

questions.text: Many people choose to have a flu vaccine, which also reduces the spread of flu to other people. What type of externality is this? Give the term.

feedback.negative externality: A negative externality is a COST to third parties
feedback.negative: A negative externality is a COST to third parties
feedback.external cost: An external cost is a negative externality — here third parties gain

questions.solution: Other people benefit without paying, so this is a positive externality (external benefit)
questions.hint: Third parties gain something good

questions.text: At a price of £3, quantity demanded is 500 units and quantity supplied is 800 units. At £2, both are 650 units. At £1, quantity demanded is 800 units and quantity supplied is 400 units. What is the equilibrium price?

options: There is no equilibrium price
feedback: At £3 there is excess supply (800 supplied, 500 demanded)
At £1 there is excess demand (800 demanded, 400 supplied)

questions.solution: At £2, quantity demanded (650) equals quantity supplied (650), so £2 is the equilibrium price
questions.hint: Find the price where the two quantities are equal

questions.text: At a price of £5, quantity demanded is 200 units and quantity supplied is 350 units. What is the situation in the market, and what is likely to happen to the price?

options: Excess supply of 150 units, so the price is likely to fall
Excess demand of 150 units, so the price is likely to rise
Excess supply of 150 units, so the price is likely to rise
The market is in equilibrium

questions.solution: Supply (350) exceeds demand (200) by 150 units; sellers cut prices to get rid of the surplus
questions.hint: Compare the two quantities, then think about what sellers do with unsold stock

questions.text: Demand for electric cars rises and, at the same time, new technology cuts the cost of making them. Which outcome is certain?

options: Price and quantity both definitely rise
The quantity sold rises, but the effect on price depends on the size of each shift
Price definitely falls and quantity falls
Neither price nor quantity changes

questions.solution: Demand shifts right (pushing price up) and supply shifts right (pushing price down); both raise quantity, but the price effect is unclear
questions.hint: Work out the effect of each shift separately, then combine them

questions.text: A government sets a maximum rent below the equilibrium rent. What is the likely result?

options: A surplus of rented homes
Rents rise above the equilibrium
A shortage of rented homes, because demand is greater than supply at that rent
No change in the market

questions.solution: Below equilibrium, more people want to rent and landlords supply fewer homes, creating excess demand
questions.hint: Compare demand and supply at a price below equilibrium

questions.text: When the price of a video game rose by 10%, the quantity demanded fell by 2%. Is demand for the game price elastic or price inelastic? Type 'elastic' or 'inelastic'.

feedback.elastic: The quantity changed by LESS (2%) than the price (10%), so demand is inelastic
feedback.price elastic: The quantity changed by LESS (2%) than the price (10%), so demand is inelastic
feedback.elastic demand: The quantity changed by LESS (2%) than the price (10%), so demand is inelastic

questions.solution: PED = -2 ÷ 10 = -0.2. Its size is less than 1, so demand is price inelastic
questions.hint: Compare the size of the change in quantity with the size of the change in price

questions.text: Explain how the price mechanism removes a shortage in a market.

rubric.model_answer: A shortage (excess demand) means quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied at the current price. Buyers compete for the limited goods, so sellers can raise the price. The higher price rations the goods: some buyers are no longer willing to pay, so quantity demanded falls. It also acts as a signal and incentive to producers: higher prices mean more profit, so quantity supplied rises. The price keeps rising until demand equals supply at the new equilibrium price.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: shortage defined (demand greater than supply)
1 mark: the price rises
1 mark: quantity demanded falls (rationing)
1 mark: quantity supplied rises (incentive/signal), reaching equilibrium
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: Excess demand pushes up the price; demand contracts and supply extends until the market reaches equilibrium
questions.hint: Start with what a shortage is, then follow what happens to the price

questions.text: Which statement about price elasticity of demand is accurate?

options: If demand is price elastic, a price rise will increase total revenue
Necessities usually have price elastic demand
Goods with many close substitutes usually have price inelastic demand
If demand is price inelastic, a price rise will increase total revenue
feedback: With elastic demand, quantity falls by more than the price rises, so revenue falls
Necessities usually have inelastic demand
Many substitutes make demand more elastic

questions.solution: With inelastic demand, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so total revenue rises
questions.hint: Think about what happens to price × quantity when quantity hardly changes

questions.text: Why might a free market fail to provide street lighting?

options: It is a public good, so people can benefit without paying (the free-rider problem)
It is a demerit good that is over-consumed
Its price is kept too low by a subsidy
It has too many sellers

questions.solution: Because nobody can be excluded, people can free-ride, so private firms cannot charge for it and will not supply it
questions.hint: Could a firm stop people who have not paid from using the light?

questions.text: Which statement about monopoly is accurate?

options: A monopoly always charges lower prices than competitive firms
A monopoly may charge higher prices and offer less choice because it faces little competition
A monopoly is a market with many small firms
A monopoly can never make a profit

questions.solution: With little competition a monopoly has market power, so it may raise prices, restrict output and reduce choice
questions.hint: Think about what happens when a firm has no rivals

questions.text: Which of these would cause the supply curve for wheat to shift to the right?

options: A rise in the price of wheat
A new tax on wheat producers
New machinery that lowers the cost of harvesting
A drought
feedback: A change in the good's own price is a movement along the supply curve
A tax raises costs and shifts supply to the left
A drought reduces supply, shifting it to the left

questions.solution: Lower costs of production increase supply at every price, shifting the curve to the right
questions.hint: A rightward shift means more is supplied at every price

questions.text: What term describes a market dominated by a few large firms, such as the UK supermarket industry? Give the term.

feedback.monopoly: A monopoly has a single dominant seller — here there are a few large firms
feedback.monopsony: A monopsony has a single dominant BUYER

questions.solution: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large firms, which watch and react to each other's decisions
questions.hint: 'Oligo' means 'few'

questions.text: Assess whether a government should use taxes or regulation to reduce pollution from factories.

rubric.model_answer: A tax on pollution makes firms pay for the external cost, giving them an incentive to cut pollution in the cheapest way, and it raises revenue that can be spent on clean-up. But the right tax level is hard to judge, demand may be inelastic, and firms may pass costs to consumers. Regulation, such as legal limits or bans, gives certain results and is easy to understand, but it needs inspection and enforcement, gives no reason to pollute less than the limit, and fines may be too small. A mix of both is often used.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: how a tax works (internalises the external cost)
1 mark: an advantage of taxes (incentive, revenue)
1 mark: a disadvantage of taxes (hard to set, inelastic demand)
1 mark: an advantage of regulation (certainty)
1 mark: a disadvantage of regulation (enforcement cost, no incentive to do better)
1 mark: a justified conclusion
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: Taxes give incentives and revenue but are hard to set; regulation is certain but costly to enforce. Often a mix is best
questions.hint: Give an advantage and a disadvantage of each, then decide

questions.text: What term describes splitting production into separate tasks, with each worker doing one task? Give the term.
questions.solution: Division of labour (specialisation of workers) breaks production into tasks so each worker becomes skilled at one
questions.hint: Adam Smith described this in a pin factory

questions.text: What term describes the fall in average cost that a firm gets as it grows larger? Give the term.

feedback.diseconomies of scale: Diseconomies of scale make average cost RISE as a firm grows too large

questions.solution: Economies of scale are the cost advantages of growing larger, which lower average cost
questions.hint: The cost benefits come from the 'scale' of production

questions.text: What is productivity?

options: Output per worker (or per hour worked)
The total number of workers in a firm
The total revenue of a firm
The price of a product

questions.solution: Labour productivity = total output ÷ number of workers (or hours worked)
questions.hint: It measures how much each worker produces

questions.text: Which of these is a fixed cost for a bakery?

options: Flour
Rent for the shop
Packaging for each loaf
Eggs for the cakes

questions.solution: Fixed costs do not change with output (rent); variable costs rise with output (flour, packaging, eggs)
questions.hint: Which cost stays the same however much bread is baked?

questions.text: Which economist described specialisation in a pin factory in 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776)?

options: Karl Marx
John Maynard Keynes
Adam Smith
Milton Friedman

questions.solution: Adam Smith showed that dividing pin-making into separate tasks greatly increased output per worker
questions.hint: He was an 18th-century Scottish economist

questions.text: What term describes a firm aiming to make the largest possible difference between its revenue and its costs? Give the term.
questions.solution: Profit maximisation is the traditional objective of firms: making as much profit as possible
questions.hint: Profit = revenue − costs; the firm wants the biggest possible amount

questions.text: Which is an example of a purchasing economy of scale?

options: A large firm can borrow money at lower interest rates
A large firm can afford specialist managers
A large firm finds communication harder
A large firm gets discounts by buying raw materials in bulk
feedback: That is a financial economy of scale
That is a managerial economy of scale
That is a diseconomy of scale

questions.solution: Buying in bulk gives lower prices per unit: a purchasing (bulk-buying) economy of scale
questions.hint: 'Purchasing' means buying

questions.text: Which is a diseconomy of scale?

options: Communication becomes slower and harder as the firm grows
Bulk buying lowers the cost of each unit
The firm can afford better technology
Banks offer the firm cheaper loans

questions.solution: Diseconomies of scale (poor communication, coordination and motivation) can raise average costs in very large firms
questions.hint: Look for a problem that comes from being very big

questions.text: Which describes capital-intensive production?

options: Production that uses a lot of workers compared with machinery
Production that uses a lot of machinery compared with workers
Production that uses no machines
Production that happens only in the public sector
feedback: That describes labour-intensive production

questions.solution: Capital-intensive production relies mainly on machinery (e.g. car assembly); labour-intensive relies mainly on workers
questions.hint: In economics, 'capital' means machinery and equipment

questions.text: A firm aims to make 'enough' profit to keep its owners happy, rather than the maximum possible. What is this called?

options: Profit maximisation
Revenue maximisation
Satisficing
Survival

questions.solution: Satisficing means aiming for a satisfactory level of profit, often because managers have other goals too
questions.hint: The word combines 'satisfy' and 'suffice'

questions.text: What term describes two firms agreeing to join together to form one new firm? Give the term.

feedback.takeover: A takeover is when one firm buys control of another — here the firms agree to join together
feedback.acquisition: An acquisition is when one firm buys another — here the firms agree to join together

questions.solution: A merger is when firms agree to combine; a takeover is when one firm buys control of another
questions.hint: The two firms 'merge' into one

questions.text: What term describes a firm growing by opening new branches or increasing its own output, rather than joining with other firms? Give the term.

feedback.external growth: External growth happens through mergers and takeovers
feedback.inorganic growth: Inorganic growth happens through mergers and takeovers

questions.solution: Organic (internal) growth comes from within the firm; external growth comes from mergers and takeovers
questions.hint: This growth comes from within the firm, like a plant growing naturally

questions.text: A car maker buys a tyre company that supplies it. What type of integration is this?

options: Forward vertical integration
Horizontal integration
Conglomerate integration
Backward vertical integration
feedback: Forward integration means buying a business at a LATER stage, such as a car dealer

questions.solution: Buying a supplier (an earlier stage of production) is backward vertical integration
questions.hint: Is the tyre company before or after the car maker in the chain of production?

questions.text: A supermarket chain takes over another supermarket chain. What type of integration is this?

options: Horizontal integration
Backward vertical integration
Forward vertical integration
Conglomerate integration

questions.solution: Joining a firm at the same stage of the same industry is horizontal integration
questions.hint: Are the two firms at the same stage of production?

questions.text: A factory produced 2,000 units a week with 50 workers. After training, it produced 2,400 units a week with the same 50 workers. What has happened?

options: Labour productivity has fallen
Labour productivity has risen
The firm has employed more workers
Fixed costs have fallen

questions.solution: Output per worker rose from 2,000 ÷ 50 = 40 to 2,400 ÷ 50 = 48 units, so labour productivity rose
questions.hint: Work out the output per worker before and after

questions.text: A clothing firm gives each worker one task, such as sewing sleeves, all day. What is a likely disadvantage?

options: Output per worker always falls
Workers become skilled at every task
Workers may get bored, which can lower motivation
The firm needs no machines

questions.solution: Repetitive single tasks can be boring, lowering motivation and quality; this is a drawback of the division of labour
questions.hint: Think about how it feels to do the same task all day

questions.text: A firm makes 600 units a day with 20 workers. Calculate labour productivity in units per worker per day. Give the number.
questions.solution: Labour productivity = 600 ÷ 20 = 30 units per worker per day
questions.hint: Divide the total output by the number of workers

questions.text: A chocolate maker buys a chain of sweet shops that sell its products. Is this forward or backward vertical integration? Type 'forward' or 'backward'.

feedback.backward: Backward integration means buying a SUPPLIER, which is an earlier stage
feedback.backward vertical integration: Backward integration means buying a SUPPLIER, which is an earlier stage
feedback.backward integration: Backward integration means buying a SUPPLIER, which is an earlier stage

questions.solution: The shops are at a later stage (closer to the customer), so this is forward vertical integration
questions.hint: Are the shops closer to the customer or closer to the raw materials?

questions.text: A firm's total cost is £200 for 10 units, £300 for 20 units and £390 for 30 units. What happens to average cost as output rises from 10 to 30 units?

options: It rises from £20 to £39 per unit
It stays at £20 per unit
It falls from £200 to £130 per unit
It falls from £20 to £13 per unit

questions.solution: Average cost = total cost ÷ output: £200 ÷ 10 = £20, £300 ÷ 20 = £15, £390 ÷ 30 = £13
questions.hint: Divide each total cost by its output

questions.text: Why might a large supermarket chain be able to charge lower prices than a small corner shop?

options: It benefits from economies of scale, such as bulk buying
It has higher average costs
It pays no rent
It faces no competition

questions.solution: Economies of scale lower the supermarket's average costs, so it can charge lower prices and still make a profit
questions.hint: Think about why bigger firms often have lower costs per unit

questions.text: A firm's workers become 10% more productive, but wages stay the same. What happens to the labour cost of making each unit?

options: It rises
It falls
It stays the same
It doubles

questions.solution: The same wage bill now produces more units, so the labour cost per unit falls
questions.hint: The firm pays the same wages but gets more output

questions.text: Which is an example of an external economy of scale?

options: A firm buys materials in bulk
A firm employs specialist managers
A pool of skilled workers develops in an area where many similar firms are based
A firm uses its own larger machines
feedback: Bulk buying is an internal economy of scale
Specialist managers are an internal economy of scale

questions.solution: External economies come from the growth of the industry in an area (skilled labour, specialist suppliers), not from the firm itself
questions.hint: External means coming from outside the firm

questions.text: A firm's total cost of producing 400 units is £2,000. Calculate the average cost per unit in pounds. Give the number.
questions.solution: Average cost = total cost ÷ output = £2,000 ÷ 400 = £5 per unit
questions.hint: Divide the total cost by the number of units

questions.text: Explain two economies of scale that a growing firm might benefit from.

rubric.model_answer: First, purchasing (bulk-buying) economies: a larger firm buys raw materials in large quantities, so suppliers give discounts and the cost of each unit falls. Second, technical economies: a larger firm can afford expensive, efficient machinery and spread its cost over a much larger output, lowering average cost. Other examples include financial economies (borrowing more cheaply) and managerial economies (hiring specialist managers).
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: first economy of scale identified
1 mark: first explained, linked to lower average cost
1 mark: second economy of scale identified
1 mark: second explained, linked to lower average cost
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: E.g. bulk buying (cheaper inputs) and technical economies (efficient machinery spread over more output) lower average cost
questions.hint: Name each economy of scale, then explain why it lowers the cost of each unit

questions.text: Which statement about economies of scale is accurate?

options: Economies of scale make average costs rise as a firm grows
Only small firms benefit from economies of scale
Economies of scale raise the price of raw materials
Beyond a certain size, a firm may suffer diseconomies of scale and its average costs may rise

questions.solution: Growth lowers average costs at first, but very large firms can face diseconomies (communication, coordination, motivation)
questions.hint: Can a firm grow too big?

questions.text: A firm replaces 30 workers with machines. Which is a likely effect on the firm's costs?

options: Higher fixed costs but lower labour costs per unit
Lower fixed costs and higher wage costs
No change to costs
Higher variable costs from extra wages

questions.solution: Machines are a large fixed cost, but they reduce the wage bill and can lower the labour cost of each unit
questions.hint: Machines cost a lot to buy but replace wages

questions.text: Why might a newly opened business aim for survival rather than profit maximisation?

options: It is legally banned from making a profit
It may not yet have enough customers to cover its costs
Survival always brings the highest profit
It has no costs in its first year

questions.solution: New firms face high start-up costs and few customers, so staying in business comes before maximising profit
questions.hint: Think about the risks a new business faces

questions.text: Which is a disadvantage of specialisation for a whole economy?

options: It always lowers output
It means each worker learns every skill
Relying on a few industries makes it vulnerable if demand for them falls
It stops countries from trading

questions.solution: If an economy specialises in a few industries, a fall in demand for them can cause high unemployment
questions.hint: Think about what happens if the main industry declines

questions.text: A firm's aim is to sell as many units as possible so that it has the largest share of its market. Which objective is this? Give the term.
questions.solution: Aiming for the largest share of sales in a market is a market share (or sales maximisation) objective
questions.hint: The aim is about the firm's percentage of all sales in the market

questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of specialisation (the division of labour) for a firm.

rubric.model_answer: Advantages: workers become skilled and quick at one task, so output per worker (productivity) rises and average costs fall. Less training is needed for each task, and specialist machinery can be used. Disadvantages: repetitive work can be boring, lowering motivation and quality; if one stage breaks down or a worker is absent, the whole process can stop; and workers have narrow skills. Overall, specialisation usually raises productivity, but firms may need job rotation to keep workers motivated.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: advantage identified (e.g. higher productivity)
1 mark: advantage explained (e.g. lower average cost)
1 mark: disadvantage identified (e.g. boredom)
1 mark: disadvantage explained (e.g. lower motivation or quality)
1 mark: second disadvantage (e.g. dependence on each stage)
1 mark: a balanced conclusion
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: Advantages: higher productivity and lower costs. Disadvantages: boredom, lower motivation, dependence on each stage
questions.hint: Give at least two advantages and two disadvantages, then conclude

questions.text: Which of these is a function of money?

options: Medium of exchange
Factor of production
Cause of inflation
Type of tax

questions.solution: Money's functions are a medium of exchange, a store of value, a unit of account and a standard of deferred payment
questions.hint: Money is used to buy and sell

questions.text: What term describes swapping goods or services directly for other goods or services, without using money? Give the term.
questions.solution: Barter is direct exchange; it needs a double coincidence of wants, which money removes
questions.hint: It is how people traded before money

questions.text: What is the reward for saving money in a bank account?

options: Profit
Interest
Rent
Wages

questions.solution: Savers receive interest; borrowers pay interest
questions.hint: The bank pays you for using your money

questions.text: What is the name of the UK's central bank? Give the name.
questions.solution: The Bank of England is the UK's central bank; its Monetary Policy Committee sets Bank Rate
questions.hint: It is based in Threadneedle Street in London

questions.text: What is a trade union?

options: A group of firms that agree to fix prices
A government department that sets taxes
An organisation that represents workers and bargains for better pay and conditions
A bank that lends to businesses

questions.solution: Trade unions represent their members in negotiations with employers about pay and conditions
questions.hint: Its members are workers

questions.text: What term describes pay before any deductions, such as income tax, are taken off? Give the term.

feedback.net pay: Net pay is what is left AFTER deductions
feedback.net income: Net income is what is left AFTER deductions
feedback.net: Net pay is what is left AFTER deductions

questions.solution: Gross pay is the full amount before deductions; net pay is what is left after them
questions.hint: It is the 'whole' amount earned

questions.text: Which is a role of the Bank of England (a central bank)?

options: Opening current accounts for members of the public
Selling car insurance
Running high-street shops
Setting the base interest rate for the economy
feedback: Commercial (high-street) banks open accounts for the public

questions.solution: The central bank sets the base interest rate (Bank Rate), issues banknotes and acts as the government's bank
questions.hint: A central bank looks after the whole economy, not individual customers

questions.text: What is collective bargaining?

options: A trade union negotiating pay and conditions with employers on behalf of its members
Customers bargaining over prices in a market
Banks agreeing interest rates with each other
Each worker negotiating their own pay alone

questions.solution: In collective bargaining, a union negotiates for all its members together, which gives them more power
questions.hint: 'Collective' means as a group

questions.text: Which deduction from pay helps to fund state benefits such as the State Pension?

options: VAT
National Insurance contributions
Council tax
Corporation tax
feedback: VAT is a tax on spending, not a deduction from pay
Corporation tax is paid by companies on their profits

questions.solution: National Insurance contributions are taken from pay and build entitlement to the State Pension and some benefits
questions.hint: It has 'insurance' in its name

questions.text: Which statement about savers and borrowers is accurate?

options: Savers pay interest; borrowers receive interest
Interest rates do not affect savers or borrowers
Savers receive interest; borrowers pay interest
Only firms pay interest

questions.solution: Interest is the reward for saving and the cost of borrowing
questions.hint: Who is the bank paying, and who is paying the bank?

questions.text: What term describes pay after deductions such as income tax and National Insurance have been taken off? Give the term.
questions.solution: Net (take-home) pay = gross pay − deductions such as income tax, National Insurance and pension contributions
questions.hint: It is the amount the worker actually takes home

questions.text: What term describes action taken by workers, such as going on strike, to put pressure on an employer? Give the term.
questions.solution: Industrial action includes strikes, work-to-rule and overtime bans
questions.hint: This kind of action happens in industry and workplaces

questions.text: Interest rates rise. What is the likely effect on household borrowing?

options: Borrowing rises because loans become cheaper
Borrowing is unaffected
Borrowing rises because saving becomes less attractive
Borrowing falls because loans become more expensive

questions.solution: Higher interest rates raise the cost of loans and credit, so households borrow less
questions.hint: Interest is the price of borrowing

questions.text: Doctors are usually paid more than shop assistants. Which reason explains this?

options: Doctors need many years of training and their skills are scarce
There are more doctors than shop assistants
Shop assistants always work longer hours than doctors
Doctors never belong to trade unions

questions.solution: The supply of qualified doctors is limited by long training, and demand for their skills is high, so wages are high
questions.hint: Think about the supply of people who can do each job

questions.text: Demand for a firm's product falls, so the firm needs fewer workers. Which idea explains this?

options: Wages have risen
Demand for labour is derived from demand for the product
Workers have joined a trade union
Interest rates have fallen

questions.solution: Firms want workers in order to make goods, so the demand for labour is derived demand
questions.hint: Why does a firm employ workers in the first place?

questions.text: Which change would encourage people to save more?

options: Interest rates on savings fall
Their income falls sharply
Interest rates on savings rise
Borrowing becomes cheaper

questions.solution: A higher interest rate increases the reward for saving
questions.hint: What makes saving more rewarding?

questions.text: Aisha earns £20 per hour and works 30 hours a week. What is her gross weekly pay in pounds? Give the number.
questions.solution: Gross weekly pay = £20 × 30 hours = £600
questions.hint: Multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours

questions.text: Which function of money means it can be used to measure and compare the value of different goods? Give the term.

feedback.store of value: A store of value means money keeps its value over time so it can be saved
feedback.medium of exchange: A medium of exchange means money is accepted in payment for goods

questions.solution: As a unit of account (measure of value), money lets us compare values, e.g. a coat costs the same as 10 cinema tickets
questions.hint: Prices let us compare the worth of different things

questions.text: A worker's gross pay is £2,400 a month. Deductions are income tax £280, National Insurance £150 and pension £120. What is the worker's net pay?

feedback: Include the pension contribution too
Deductions are taken away, not added

questions.hint: Add up all the deductions, then subtract them from gross pay

questions.text: A trade union wins a large pay rise for its members. What is a possible disadvantage for workers?

options: The firm may employ fewer workers because labour costs have risen
All workers will be paid less
The firm's costs will fall
Workers will have to work longer hours for no pay

questions.solution: Higher wages raise costs, so the firm may cut jobs or replace workers with machines
questions.hint: Think about the firm's costs after the pay rise

questions.text: Which change would increase the supply of labour to an industry?

options: A fall in wages in the industry
More people gaining the qualifications needed for the job
Worse working conditions
Longer and more expensive training for the job

questions.solution: If more people are qualified and able to do the job, the supply of labour increases
questions.hint: Supply of labour means the number of people willing and able to do the job

questions.text: The Bank of England cuts interest rates. Which group is most likely to lose out?

options: Borrowers, because loans cost more
Homeowners with variable-rate mortgages
Savers, because they earn less interest
Firms planning to borrow to invest
feedback: Lower interest rates make loans CHEAPER
Their mortgage payments are likely to fall
Cheaper loans help firms that want to borrow

questions.solution: Lower rates reduce the return on savings; borrowers, including those with variable-rate mortgages, gain
questions.hint: Who receives interest?

questions.text: Suppose the first £12,000 of a person's yearly income is tax-free and the rest is taxed at 20%. A worker earns £15,000 a year. How much income tax do they pay in a year? Give the number of pounds.
questions.hint: Work out how much income is above the tax-free amount first

questions.text: Explain two factors that affect the wage a worker is paid.

rubric.model_answer: First, skills and qualifications: jobs needing long training, such as doctors, have a small supply of qualified workers, so wages are high. Second, the demand for labour: if demand for the product is high and workers are very productive, firms are willing to pay more. Other factors include trade union power, which can bargain wages up, the minimum wage, the danger or unpleasantness of the job, and where the job is located.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: first factor identified
1 mark: first factor explained (link to supply or demand of labour)
1 mark: second factor identified
1 mark: second factor explained
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: E.g. skills/qualifications (limit supply) and demand for the product or productivity (raise demand); also unions and the minimum wage
questions.hint: Think about the supply of workers and the demand for workers

questions.text: Which statement about a national minimum wage is accurate?

options: It always increases the number of jobs
It lowers the pay of the lowest-paid workers
It applies only to self-employed people
It may raise the pay of low-paid workers, but could reduce the number of jobs if it is set too high

questions.solution: A minimum wage protects low-paid workers, but if it is above the market wage, firms may demand fewer workers
questions.hint: Think about both workers and employers

questions.text: Which statement explains why higher interest rates can reduce consumer spending?

options: Borrowing costs more and saving is more rewarding, so people spend less
Prices of goods fall immediately
Incomes rise for all households
Firms must lower their prices by law

questions.solution: Higher rates make loans and mortgages dearer and saving more attractive, so consumer spending falls
questions.hint: Think about the effect on both borrowers and savers

questions.text: Why might a trade union have less bargaining power in an industry where many unemployed people have the right skills?

options: Unions are banned when unemployment is high
Employers can more easily find other workers, so the union's threats carry less weight
Unemployed people must join the union
Wages are always set by the government

questions.solution: When there is a large supply of suitable workers, employers depend less on the union's members, weakening its bargaining power
questions.hint: Think about how easily the employer could find other staff

questions.text: Which problem of barter does money solve?

options: The need for goods to be produced
The need for people to work
The need for a double coincidence of wants
The scarcity of resources

questions.solution: With barter you must find someone who has what you want AND wants what you have; money removes this problem
questions.hint: In barter, both people must want what the other has

questions.text: What term describes the demand for labour depending on the demand for the goods and services that labour produces? Give the term.
questions.solution: Labour is a derived demand: firms employ workers because consumers want the products they make
questions.hint: The demand for workers is 'drawn' from the demand for products

questions.text: Discuss whether higher interest rates are good for households.

rubric.model_answer: Higher interest rates help households that save, because they earn more interest, and they can reduce inflation, protecting the value of incomes. However, households with loans, credit cards or variable-rate mortgages face higher repayments, leaving less to spend. Higher rates can also slow the economy, so firms may cut jobs, which harms households. Overall, the effect depends on whether a household is mainly a saver or a borrower: savers gain, borrowers lose.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: a benefit identified (e.g. savers earn more interest)
1 mark: the benefit explained
1 mark: a cost identified (e.g. higher loan or mortgage repayments)
1 mark: the cost explained (less disposable income)
1 mark: a wider effect (lower inflation or fewer jobs)
1 mark: a judgement (depends on saver or borrower)
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: Savers gain more interest and inflation may fall; borrowers pay more and jobs may be lost. It depends on the household
questions.hint: Consider savers and borrowers separately, then decide

questions.text: What is the name of the measure of the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year? Give the abbreviation or the full name.
questions.solution: Gross domestic product (GDP) measures a country's total output; a rise in real GDP is economic growth
questions.hint: It is a three-letter abbreviation that starts with G

questions.text: What is inflation?

options: A sustained rise in the general price level
A fall in the general price level
A rise in unemployment
A rise in the value of the pound
feedback: A fall in the general price level is deflation

questions.solution: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general level of prices, which reduces the purchasing power of money
questions.hint: Think about what happens to prices over time

questions.text: What term describes a sustained fall in the general price level? Give the term.

feedback.disinflation: Disinflation is when prices are still rising, but more slowly
feedback.inflation: Inflation is a RISE in the general price level

questions.solution: Deflation means the general price level is falling
questions.hint: It is the opposite of inflation

questions.text: Which of these is a direct tax?

options: VAT
Income tax
Excise duty on petrol
A tariff on imports
feedback: VAT is an indirect tax on spending
Excise duty is an indirect tax on spending

questions.solution: Direct taxes are paid directly to the government from income or profit (income tax, corporation tax); indirect taxes are on spending
questions.hint: A direct tax is taken from what people earn

questions.text: What term describes the government using its spending and taxation to influence the economy? Give the term.

feedback.monetary policy: Monetary policy uses interest rates and the money supply
feedback.monetary: Monetary policy uses interest rates and the money supply

questions.solution: Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxation; monetary policy uses interest rates and the money supply
questions.hint: It involves the government's budget

questions.text: What is an export?

options: A good or service bought from another country
A tax on imported goods
A good or service sold to buyers in another country
A limit on the quantity of imports
feedback: That is an import
That is a tariff
That is a quota

questions.solution: Exports are sold abroad and bring money into the country; imports are bought from abroad
questions.hint: 'Ex' means out

questions.text: Which is an example of monetary policy?

options: Changing income tax rates
Building new hospitals
Changing the rate of VAT
Changing interest rates
feedback: Changing taxes is fiscal policy
Government spending is fiscal policy
Changing taxes is fiscal policy

questions.solution: Monetary policy uses interest rates and the money supply; tax and spending changes are fiscal policy
questions.hint: Monetary policy is about money and interest

questions.text: Which type of unemployment happens when people are between jobs, for example after leaving one job and while searching for another?

options: Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
feedback: Structural unemployment is caused by the long-term decline of industries
Cyclical unemployment is caused by a fall in demand during a recession

questions.solution: Frictional unemployment is short-term unemployment while people move between jobs
questions.hint: It is caused by the time it takes to move smoothly from one job to another

questions.text: What is a tariff?

options: A limit on the number of goods imported
A tax on imported goods
A subsidy given to exporters
A ban on all trade
feedback: A limit on quantity is a quota

questions.solution: A tariff is a tax on imports; a quota is a limit on the quantity of imports
questions.hint: It is a form of tax

questions.text: Which of these is a measure of inflation?

options: The FTSE 100 share index
The Human Development Index
The Consumer Prices Index (CPI)
Gross domestic product
feedback: The FTSE 100 tracks share prices of large companies
GDP measures total output, not prices

questions.solution: The Consumer Prices Index tracks the prices of a typical basket of goods and services over time
questions.hint: Look for an index based on prices that consumers pay

questions.text: What term describes unemployment caused by the long-term decline of an industry, such as coal mining, when workers' skills no longer match the jobs available? Give the term.

feedback.cyclical unemployment: Cyclical unemployment is caused by a recession
feedback.cyclical: Cyclical unemployment is caused by a recession
feedback.frictional unemployment: Frictional unemployment is short-term, between jobs
feedback.frictional: Frictional unemployment is short-term, between jobs
feedback.seasonal unemployment: Seasonal unemployment happens at certain times of year
feedback.seasonal: Seasonal unemployment happens at certain times of year

questions.solution: Structural unemployment comes from long-term changes in the structure of the economy
questions.hint: The 'structure' of the economy has changed

questions.text: What term describes a rise in the value of a currency against other currencies, caused by the market? Give the term.

feedback.depreciation: A depreciation is a FALL in a currency's value
feedback.devaluation: A devaluation is a deliberate FALL in a currency's value

questions.solution: An appreciation is a rise in a currency's value; a depreciation is a fall
questions.hint: When something rises in value, we say it ...

questions.text: The pound appreciates against the euro. What happens to the price of UK exports for buyers in the eurozone?

options: They become cheaper
They do not change
They can no longer be sold
They become more expensive

questions.solution: A stronger pound means eurozone buyers need more euros to buy each pound, so UK exports become dearer (Strong Pound: Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer)
questions.hint: Each pound now costs more euros

questions.text: The government cuts income tax. What is the likely effect on consumer spending?

options: It rises, because people have more disposable income
It falls, because people have less income
It stays the same
It falls, because prices rise immediately

questions.solution: Lower income tax raises disposable income, so consumers are likely to spend more
questions.hint: What happens to take-home pay when income tax is cut?

questions.text: Ski instructors in a mountain resort are out of work every summer. What type of unemployment is this?

options: Structural unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Cyclical unemployment

questions.solution: Seasonal unemployment happens because demand for some jobs changes with the time of year
questions.hint: Think about the time of year

questions.text: A country spends more on imports of goods and services than it earns from exports. What does this mean for its balance of trade?

options: It has a trade surplus
Its trade is balanced
It has a trade deficit
It has no trade
feedback: A surplus means exports are greater than imports

questions.solution: Imports greater than exports means a trade deficit
questions.hint: Balance of trade = exports − imports: is the result positive or negative?

questions.text: Total demand in the economy rises faster than the economy can produce goods and services, so prices rise. What type of inflation is this? Give the term.

feedback.cost-push inflation: Cost-push inflation is caused by rising costs of production
feedback.cost push inflation: Cost-push inflation is caused by rising costs of production
feedback.cost-push: Cost-push inflation is caused by rising costs of production
feedback.cost push: Cost-push inflation is caused by rising costs of production

questions.solution: Demand-pull inflation: too much spending chasing too few goods 'pulls' prices up
questions.hint: Prices are being 'pulled' up by spending

questions.text: A country has two consecutive quarters of negative economic growth. What is this called? Give the term.

feedback.depression: A depression is a much deeper and longer downturn — two quarters of falling output has a different name

questions.solution: A recession is commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP
questions.hint: It is the downturn phase of the economic cycle

questions.text: Real GDP growth in four quarters was: Q1 +0.5%, Q2 +0.2%, Q3 −0.3%, Q4 −0.1%. Which conclusion is correct?

options: Real GDP fell in every quarter
Real GDP rose in every quarter
Real GDP fell only in Q1
Real GDP fell in Q3 and Q4, so the economy was in recession

questions.solution: Growth was negative in two consecutive quarters (Q3 and Q4), which meets the usual definition of a recession
questions.hint: Look for negative growth figures in a row

questions.text: A basket of goods cost £200 last year and £210 this year. What is the rate of inflation for this basket?

feedback: £10 is the change in pounds — turn it into a percentage of the original £200
That's this year's cost as a percentage of last year's — the rise is the part above 100%
Divide by last year's price (£200), not this year's

questions.solution: Change = £10. Inflation = £10 ÷ £200 × 100 = 5%
questions.hint: Divide the change in price by last year's price, then multiply by 100

questions.text: Why might a fall in the value of the pound increase inflation in the UK?

options: Exports become more expensive
Imported goods and raw materials become more expensive
Interest rates automatically fall
Unemployment falls to zero
feedback: A weaker pound makes exports CHEAPER for foreign buyers

questions.solution: A weaker pound makes imports dearer, raising firms' costs and the prices of imported goods
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the price of things bought from abroad

questions.text: Which is a supply-side policy?

options: Raising interest rates
Raising benefit payments to boost spending
Spending more on education and training to improve workers' skills
Putting a tariff on imports
feedback: Changing interest rates is monetary policy

questions.solution: Supply-side policies aim to increase the economy's productive capacity, for example by improving skills
questions.hint: Supply-side policies aim to increase how much the economy can produce

questions.text: A government spends more than it receives in tax revenue in one year. What is the name for this gap? Give the term.

feedback.national debt: The national debt is the TOTAL built up over many years — the gap in one year has a different name
feedback.budget surplus: A budget surplus is when revenue is GREATER than spending
feedback.surplus: A surplus is when revenue is GREATER than spending

questions.solution: A budget deficit is when spending is greater than revenue in a year; borrowing covers the gap
questions.hint: It is the opposite of a budget surplus

questions.text: Explain two possible causes of inflation.

rubric.model_answer: First, demand-pull inflation: if total demand in the economy grows faster than the economy can produce, for example because of rising consumer spending, firms raise prices. Second, cost-push inflation: if firms' costs rise, for example because of higher wages, energy prices or imported raw materials after a fall in the pound, they pass the higher costs on to consumers as higher prices.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: demand-pull identified
1 mark: demand-pull explained (too much demand for the available output)
1 mark: cost-push identified
1 mark: cost-push explained (higher costs passed on in prices)
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: Demand-pull (spending grows faster than output) and cost-push (rising wages, energy or import costs passed on)
questions.hint: One cause comes from spending; the other comes from firms' costs

questions.text: Which statement about economic growth is accurate?

options: It always reduces inequality
It always lowers unemployment to zero
It means the general price level is falling
It can raise living standards but may also increase pollution

questions.solution: Growth raises incomes and can create jobs, but it can also bring costs such as pollution and use of resources
questions.hint: Growth has benefits and costs

questions.text: Which statement about a progressive tax is accurate?

options: Higher earners pay a larger percentage of their income in tax
Everyone pays the same amount of tax
Lower earners pay a larger percentage of their income in tax
It is charged only on imports
feedback: That describes a regressive tax

questions.solution: With a progressive tax, the percentage of income paid rises as income rises
questions.hint: Think about the percentage of income, not the amount

questions.text: Why might protectionism, such as tariffs, harm consumers?

options: Imported goods become cheaper
Imported goods become more expensive and choice may be reduced
Domestic firms face more competition
The variety of imported goods increases

questions.solution: Tariffs raise the price of imports and reduce competition, so consumers pay more and have less choice
questions.hint: Who pays the tariff in the end?

questions.text: Which statement about globalisation is accurate?

options: It means countries trade less with each other
It has stopped multinational companies from operating
It has increased trade between countries, but some workers lose jobs when production moves abroad
It affects only the countries of Europe

questions.solution: Globalisation has increased trade, investment and links between economies, with winners and losers
questions.hint: Globalisation means the world's economies are becoming more connected

questions.text: What term describes a company that has its headquarters in one country and operates in several other countries? Give the term or its abbreviation.
questions.solution: Multinational (transnational) companies operate in many countries and are a major part of globalisation
questions.hint: 'Multi' means many and 'national' means countries

questions.text: Assess whether lowering interest rates is an effective way to reduce unemployment.

rubric.model_answer: Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper and saving less attractive, so consumers spend more and firms invest more. Higher demand means firms need more workers, so cyclical unemployment falls. However, it may take a long time to work, and if confidence is low, people may not borrow even at low rates. It does little for structural unemployment, where workers lack the right skills; training (a supply-side policy) is needed. Lower rates can also raise inflation. So it works best for unemployment caused by a recession.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: lower rates make borrowing cheaper / saving less attractive
1 mark: spending and investment rise
1 mark: firms need more workers, so cyclical unemployment falls
1 mark: a limitation (time lags, low confidence, inflation)
1 mark: does not solve structural unemployment
1 mark: a justified conclusion
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: It can cut cyclical unemployment by boosting spending, but works slowly, may raise inflation and does not fix structural unemployment
questions.hint: Explain the chain of effects, then its limits, then decide
